articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: The descending genicular artery (DGA) is relevant to genicular artery embolization (GAE), medial femoral condyle and perforator flaps, recipient-vessel selection, and vascular complications around the knee. This review integrated cadaveric, imaging, procedural, reconstructive, and safety evidence and examined whether bilateral cadaveric sampling affected pooled estimates. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science/SCIE, CENTRAL/Ovid, and LILACS/BVS were searched through 10 June 2026, followed by a targeted update on 18 August 2026. Evidence was stratified by design; anatomical prevalence was not pooled with in vivo visualization. Anatomical studies were appraised using an AQUA-adapted framework, imaging studies using the JBI analytical cross-sectional checklist, reconstructive series using the JBI case-series checklist, and case reports using the JBI case-report checklist. Compatible outcomes were synthesized with REML random-effects models and Knapp-Hartung confidence intervals. Results: Sixty-five primary studies were included, and 22 contributed to at least one quantitative synthesis. Strict cadaveric DGA presence was 91.6% (95% CI 86.6-94.8; I2 = 30.3%); a worst-case cluster-adjusted sensitivity estimate accounting for bilateral specimens was 89.7% (84.7-93.2%). Femoral/superficial femoral origin was 92.4% (89.2-94.7), popliteal origin 3.2% (2.2-4.6), and an articular/osteoarticular branch 90.3% (84.1-94.2). In vivo DGA visualization during GAE-related imaging was 95.9% (93.1-97.6) and was interpreted separately from anatomical prevalence. Reconstructive and safety evidence was predominantly derived from small series and case reports. Conclusions: The DGA is usually identifiable and generally arises from the femoral arterial system, but branch-level variability remains clinically important. Cadaveric anatomy and procedural imaging are complementary. The anatomical findings may inform GAE and reconstructive planning, whereas clinical safety and reconstructive conclusions require confirmation in larger cohorts.

articles.title: Beyond Conventional MRI: Molecular PET, Multiparametric MRI, and PET/MRI in Glioma Management.
articles.abstract: Despite its central clinical role, conventional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides an incomplete picture of the tumor biology of gliomas, which are biologically heterogeneous tumors. Molecular positron emission tomography (PET) with amino acid tracers, multiparametric MRI techniques (perfusion-, diffusion-, and spectroscopy-based sequences), and hybrid PET/MRI have each been proposed to overcome specific limitations of anatomic imaging in diagnosis, treatment planning, and posttreatment assessment. This narrative review examined the current evidence for molecular PET, multiparametric MRI, and integrated PET/MRI across the glioma care pathway. Rather than framing these modalities as competing alternatives, we argue that amino acid transport, vascularity, water diffusion, and metabolite composition capture distinct and often spatially incongruent facets of tumor biology, such that discordance between modalities may reflect the underlying tumor heterogeneity. We also summarized the guideline recommendations (RANO/EANO, EANM/SNMMI, etc.), outlined current evidence gaps, and discussed emerging directions in novel PET tracers, artificial intelligence, radiomics, and theranostics. Molecular PET and multiparametric MRI should be used as modalities complementary to conventional MRI within multidisciplinary glioma care, while the choice and sequence of examinations should be guided by the clinical question.

articles.title: Renal Involvement in Down Syndrome: Developmental and Clinical Perspectives.
articles.abstract: With the increasing life expectancy of individuals with Down syndrome (DS), kidney disease has emerged as an important yet under-recognized contributor to long-term morbidity and mortality in this population. This narrative review summarizes current knowledge regarding the developmental, structural, histopathological, and clinical aspects of renal involvement in DS. A literature search was conducted, and studies addressing renal structure, function, development, or pathology in individuals with DS (clinical studies, autopsy studies, case reports, and experimental studies) were included. Available evidence indicates that renal involvement in DS extends beyond congenital anomalies to include altered nephrogenesis, acquired glomerulopathies, and progressive functional impairment. Histopathological studies of fetal kidneys suggest altered nephrogenesis and delayed renal maturation in DS, potentially resulting in reduced nephron endowment. However, the long-term functional consequences of these developmental findings remain uncertain. Reported acquired glomerular diseases are heterogeneous and include IgA nephropathy, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, membranous nephropathy, ANCA-associated glomerulonephritis, and several rarer entities. Conventional renal biomarkers may underestimate kidney dysfunction in DS because of altered body composition and reduced muscle mass, while evidence regarding novel biomarkers such as NGAL and KIM-1 remains limited. Renal involvement in DS is multifactorial and likely reflects the interplay between disturbed nephrogenesis, developmental renal abnormalities, and acquired renal disease, resulting in increased renal vulnerability throughout life. Improved awareness, earlier nephrological surveillance, and validation of sensitive renal biomarkers may facilitate earlier detection of kidney injuries and improve long-term renal outcomes in individuals with DS.

articles.title: Esophageal Injury During Transesophageal Echocardiography-Guided Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion: A Narrative Review.
articles.abstract: Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) remains an established imaging modality for guiding percutaneous left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO), providing real-time visualization during transseptal puncture, device deployment, and procedural assessment. However, esophageal instrumentation and prolonged probe manipulation may result in gastrointestinal injury, particularly in patients with pre-existing esophageal abnormalities or increased bleeding risk. This narrative review summarizes the available evidence regarding the mechanisms, risk factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis, management, and prevention of TEE-associated esophageal injury during LAAO while examining alternative imaging strategies. A literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library, supplemented by targeted searches of broader structural heart intervention literature. Although clinically recognized TEE-associated gastrointestinal complications are uncommon, studies employing systematic endoscopic surveillance have identified substantially higher rates of subclinical mucosal injury. Reported manifestations range from transient dysphagia and superficial mucosal lesions to gastrointestinal bleeding, intramural esophageal hematoma, perforation, and fistula formation. LAAO-specific registry and administrative datasets report gastrointestinal bleeding rates ranging from approximately 0.2% to 8.2%, but heterogeneous outcome definitions, ascertainment methods, and the absence of systematic endoscopic verification prevent these findings from being interpreted as rates of TEE-associated esophageal injury. Nevertheless, limited LAAO-specific evidence, heterogeneous outcome definitions, and differences in surveillance strategies preclude reliable estimation of procedure-specific esophageal injury incidence. Intracardiac echocardiography eliminates esophageal instrumentation but carries a distinct procedural risk profile, whereas cardiac computed tomography (CCT) provides complementary opportunities for preprocedural planning and postprocedural surveillance. Careful preprocedural assessment, judicious probe manipulation, early recognition of complications, and individualized imaging selection are important considerations. Prospective studies incorporating standardized esophageal injury endpoints are needed to establish the true clinical burden and guide preventive strategies.

articles.title: Gender, Age, and Ethnic Differences in Ultrasound Predictors of Malignancy Risk in Thyroid Nodules with Indeterminate Low-Risk Cytology (TIR3A): A Systematic Literature Review.
articles.abstract: Background: Thyroid nodules classified as TIR3A (Italian Reporting System) or Bethesda III (atypia of undetermined significance/follicular lesion of undetermined significance) represent a diagnostic challenge with malignancy rates of 10-30%. While ultrasound features guide risk stratification, the influence of patient demographics-particularly gender, age, and ethnicity-on ultrasound predictors of malignant transformation remains incompletely characterized. Methods: We conducted a systematic literature review of studies evaluating ultrasound features in TIR3A/Bethesda III thyroid nodules, with specific focus on gender differences (male vs. female), age-related patterns, and ethnic variations (Caucasian vs. non-Caucasian). We extracted data on malignancy rates, odds ratios, relative risks, and diagnostic performance metrics (sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, area under the curve) for individual ultrasound alarm signs stratified by demographic variables. A total of 20 studies were included (17 retrospective cohort studies, 3 prospective cohort studies); findings were synthesized qualitatively. Results: Male sex was reported as a risk modifier in small cohorts (crude relative risk 2.3; independent predictor status in one multivariate analysis without a reported adjusted odds ratio), but larger series found no significant sex effect; adjusted estimates are unavailable, and the association should be considered inconsistent and of uncertain magnitude. Age below 55 years was associated with higher malignancy rates and more aggressive ultrasound features in heterogeneous single-centre observational data; however, this threshold has not been validated for ultrasound-based malignancy prediction across populations. Direct Caucasian versus non-Caucasian comparative data are absent; observed geographic variation cannot be attributed to ethnicity given multiple confounders including iodine intake and healthcare system differences. Microcalcifications (sensitivity 32.4-87%, specificity 75-99.2%) and irregular margins (sensitivity 70%, specificity 94.9-95%) remain the most robust ultrasound predictors across demographic subgroups. Conclusions: Gender and age show associations with malignancy risk in TIR3A nodules, but these associations are inconsistent across cohorts and should not be treated as validated independent predictors. Ethnic comparative data remain insufficient. Optimal risk stratification should integrate demographic variables with ultrasound features and repeat cytology to personalize management and reduce unnecessary surgery.

articles.title: Toward Clinically Trustworthy Deep Learning in Cardiology: A Unified Mathematical Synthesis of Representation, Optimization, and Reliability.
articles.abstract: Background: Deep learning (DL) has revolutionized cardiovascular medicine by allowing for automated analysis of electrocardiography, imaging of the heart, and multimodal clinical datasets. Although there have been impressive advancements in terms of predictive performance, the deployment of DL methods in a clinical setting remains limited due to lack of sufficient mathematical understanding around the concepts of uncertainty, robustness, fairness, explainability, and generalizability. Methods: In this work, a systematic review is conducted using PRISMA principles on 79 peer-reviewed articles published from 2017 until 2025, with a unifying mathematical perspective on the notion of trustworthy deep learning in cardiology. Results: We find that there is significant discrepancy between prediction accuracy and clinical reliability, with little emphasis placed on mathematical guarantees, reproducibility of evaluation procedures, calibration, or robustness verification. To address this challenge, we propose a conceptual mathematical framework which brings together the elements of representation learning, optimization, and trustworthiness into a unified audit of AI in cardiac care. We note that the presented indices are purely theoretical and are meant to provide guidance for future standardization, and as such do not represent actual clinical metrics. Conclusions: Although our paper does not propose any new predictive algorithms, we do contribute a strong theoretical basis for the evaluation and development of clinically reliable deep learning algorithms in cardiology.

articles.title: CEUS of Focal Splenic Lesions: Enhancement Patterns and Differentiation of Benign and Malignant Disease.
articles.abstract: Focal splenic lesions are uncommon, and diagnostic experience with splenic imaging is substantially more limited than that with focal liver lesions. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) has emerged as a valuable imaging modality for the detection and differentiation of splenic lesions because it allows real-time assessment of vascularization and enhancement behavior without ionizing radiation. This narrative review summarizes the current evidence regarding CEUS findings in focal splenic lesions, with particular emphasis on the differentiation between benign and malignant lesions. Benign vascular lesions typically demonstrate arterial hyperenhancement or isoenhancement with persistent enhancement or only mild late washout, whereas malignant lesions frequently show early and progressive washout with marked hypoenhancement in the parenchymal phase. Rapid washout, particularly within the first 60 s after contrast administration, represents one of the most important imaging features associated with malignancy. Although overlap of enhancement patterns exists and standardized diagnostic criteria are still lacking, CEUS represents a valuable, radiation-free, and cost-effective imaging modality for the evaluation of focal splenic lesions. CEUS may improve diagnostic confidence, support clinical decision-making and reduce the need for additional cross-sectional imaging in selected patients.

articles.title: Circulating MicroRNAs in Lung Cancer and Pulmonary Tuberculosis: Diagnostic Potential, Shared Signatures, and Challenges in Differential Diagnosis.
articles.abstract: The differential diagnosis of lung cancer and pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) remains challenging because the diseases share clinical manifestations and radiological features, particularly in regions with a high tuberculosis burden. This narrative review evaluates circulating microRNAs (miRNAs), primarily measured in serum, plasma and extracellular-vesicle-enriched fractions, as potential adjunctive biomarkers for this differential diagnosis. The literature search was updated through 3 October 2026. Evidence was synthesized by comparator group, biological matrix, analytical methodology and validation design, distinguishing direct lung cancer-PTB comparisons from disease-control studies and prognostic or monitoring investigations. Numerous miRNAs have been associated with either disease, but shared candidates and opposite expression directions across separate studies do not establish differential diagnostic accuracy. Findings vary with patient selection, sample processing, detection platforms, normalization and reference standards. Direct blood-based comparisons remain limited and report variable discrimination. A plasma panel comprising miR-342-3p, miR-199a-3p and miR-199b-3p differentiated PTB from lung cancer with areas under the curve of 0.911 in training and 0.886 in internal split-sample validation; validation sensitivity and specificity were 87.9% and 75.9%, respectively. Its case-control design, incomplete microbiological confirmation and absence of concomitant lung cancer-PTB assessment limit clinical interpretation. Additional pleural-fluid findings concern a separate matrix and cannot be extrapolated to blood testing. Prognostic and treatment-associated findings remain exploratory and do not establish treatment-guiding or validated monitoring utility. Circulating miRNAs should therefore be considered potential adjuncts to clinical assessment, imaging, microbiological testing and histopathology. Clinical translation requires standardized assays, independent prospective validation in clinically relevant populations, and demonstration of incremental value and clinical utility within existing diagnostic pathways. Future studies should prespecify intended use, assay procedures and diagnostic thresholds, include patients with coexisting disease, and evaluate whether testing improves clinical decisions without replacing established microbiological or tissue confirmation methods.

articles.title: Photon-Counting CT in Oral and Maxillofacial Imaging: Clinical Applications, Dose Efficiency, and Future Perspectives.
articles.abstract: Photon-counting computed tomography (PCCT) is an emerging imaging technology that combines ultra-high spatial resolution, improved dose efficiency, reduced electronic noise, and intrinsic spectral imaging. These characteristics are particularly relevant to oral and maxillofacial radiology, where accurate depiction of small osseous and dental structures is often required in the presence of metallic restorations or implants. This review summarizes the technical principles of PCCT and examines its current and potential clinical applications across dental and maxillofacial imaging. Available evidence indicates that PCCT can improve visualization of fine root canal anatomy, periodontal and trabecular bone structures, peri-implant interfaces, subtle maxillofacial fractures, and complex sinonasal anatomy. Its spectral capabilities, including virtual monoenergetic imaging and material decomposition, may substantially reduce metal-related artifacts and improve tissue characterization. Early studies also suggest that PCCT can provide high diagnostic image quality at reduced radiation dose, with potential advantages in pediatric imaging and in patients requiring repeated examinations. Beyond morphology, PCCT may support quantitative applications such as bone mineral density assessment, iodine mapping, treatment planning, and the development of imaging biomarkers and artificial intelligence-based analysis. Despite these promising findings, cone-beam CT remains the preferred modality for many routine dental indications because of its accessibility, lower cost, and established clinical workflow. Current evidence for PCCT in oral and maxillofacial radiology is still limited and is largely derived from technical, experimental, and early clinical studies. Further prospective comparisons with cone-beam CT and conventional CT are needed to define task-specific diagnostic benefits, optimized protocols, radiation-dose advantages, and cost-effectiveness. PCCT is therefore best regarded as a promising complementary modality with particular value in diagnostically challenging cases that require very high spatial resolution, spectral information, or effective metal-artifact reduction. Nevertheless, most oral and maxillofacial evidence remains exploratory; improved image-quality metrics should not be equated with superior patient-level diagnostic accuracy. Direct comparisons with optimized CBCT yield heterogeneous, protocol-dependent dose and diagnostic findings. No standardized indication-specific PCCT acquisition framework currently exists for routine oral and maxillofacial imaging. Clinical implementation should therefore be conditional on demonstrable diagnostic benefit at a justified radiation dose and acceptable resource cost.

articles.title: Diagnostic Performance of Artificial Intelligence for the Detection and Segmentation of Periapical Lesions on Cone-Beam Computed Tomography: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) improves periapical lesion detection, but its interpretation is expertise-dependent. This systematic review evaluated artificial intelligence (AI) for detecting, classifying, and segmenting periapical lesions on CBCT. Methods: PubMed, the Cochrane Library, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar were searched to 12 December 2025 (PROSPERO: CRD420251184440). Studies comparing AI with an expert- or annotation-based reference standard on human CBCT scans were eligible. Risk of bias was assessed with the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2 (QUADAS-2) tool, and certainty of evidence with the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. Sensitivity and specificity were pooled with a bivariate model where complete 2 × 2 data were available, and all metrics with univariate random-effects models. Results: Eighteen studies were included (detection or classification, 16; segmentation, 6); 15 had unclear risk of bias in at least one domain, and most were retrospective and internally validated. In the bivariate model (seven studies), sensitivity was 88.2% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 77.6-94.2%) and specificity 85.1% (73.4-92.1%). Univariate pooled sensitivity was 90.9% (84.2-94.9%; 14 studies), specificity 89.7% (83.2-93.9%; 11 studies), accuracy 86.7% (78.9-92.0%; 10 studies), and F1-score 83.7% (76.4-89.1%; seven studies). The pooled lesion Dice similarity coefficient was 0.70 (0.61-0.78; six studies), indicating moderate spatial overlap with reference annotations. Heterogeneity was considerable for detection metrics (I2 = 90-96%), prediction intervals were wide (sensitivity 48-99%), and the certainty of evidence was very low. Conclusions: AI shows promising performance for CBCT-based periapical lesion detection under research conditions, whereas segmentation overlap is moderate. Equivalence to clinicians and clinical effectiveness are not established; prospective, externally validated studies with standardized reference standards are needed.

articles.title: Phasic Arterial Mechanics and Ventriculo-Arterial Dyssynchrony in Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Arterial Systole, Arterial Diastole and Pharmacological Phase Restoration.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Arterial stiffness is usually treated as a scalar load. We instead framed it as a timing problem, defining arterial diastole as compliant reservoir filling during left ventricular (LV) systole and arterial systole as elastic recoil during LV diastole, and we asked whether the two phases were measurably disturbed in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), and whether pre-specified drug classes could restore them. Methods: We searched MEDLINE/PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science from inception to 10 September 2026 (3835 records). After deduplication, 2043 records were screened and 376 full texts were assessed, of which 236 met the eligibility criteria and 84 contributed quantitative data. Random-effects meta-analyses used DerSimonian-Laird estimations with Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman confidence intervals; the risk of bias was assessed with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and Cochrane RoB 2. Results: Compared with controls without heart failure, patients with HFpEF or diastolic dysfunction with preserved ejection fraction had higher carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity (mean difference +1.72 m/s, 95% CI +0.73 to +2.70; k = 16; p = 0.002), higher brachial-ankle pulse wave velocity (+2.24 m/s, +1.38 to +3.10; k = 7; p = 0.0007), a higher augmentation index (+4.51%, +1.36 to +7.65; k = 10; p = 0.010), and a higher cardio-ankle vascular index (+1.00, +0.29 to +1.71; k = 5; p = 0.017). In randomised trials, pre-specified drug classes lowered the heart-rate-corrected augmentation index relative to comparators (-2.18%, -3.51 to -0.85; k = 11; p = 0.004), although this did not persist when ten further eligible trials were added by generic inverse variance (-1.36%, -2.78 to +0.07; k = 15; p = 0.060). They did not change carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity (-0.11 m/s, -0.40 to +0.18; k = 18; p = 0.428), an estimate that became significant when trials at an overall high risk of bias were excluded (-0.21 m/s, -0.41 to -0.02; k = 13; p = 0.036). Reflected-wave transit times did not differ significantly (-5.09 ms; k = 4), and the pooled correlation between arterial stiffness and longitudinal strain was not significant (r = -0.28, -0.65 to +0.20; k = 4; p = 0.162). Heterogeneity was substantial throughout, and 95% prediction intervals included the nulls for five of the six pooled indices, with the single exception being brachial-ankle pulse wave velocity. Conclusions: Arterial stiffness indices were on average higher in HFpEF, with substantial heterogeneity and prediction intervals that included the nulls for five of the six indices; under restrictions of clinically or haemodynamically defined HFpEF, the augmentation index differences lost significance (p = 0.071) while carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity was only marginal (p = 0.050). In randomised trials, the component that responded to current pharmacotherapy was the wave-reflection amplitude and not aortic conduit stiffness; this reduction derived entirely from hypertensive populations and did not survive the inclusion of ten additional eligible trials (-1.36%, -2.78 to +0.07; k = 15; p = 0.060). No analysis in this review demonstrated that the reflected wave was delayed. The phasic framework is therefore presented as an interpretation and hypothesis for prospective testing, and the phasic indices themselves remain critically under-reported.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Endoscopic Assessment of Response to Neoadjuvant Chemoradiotherapy in Esophageal Cancer: From Residual Disease Detection to Active Surveillance and Surgical Decision-Making.
articles.abstract: Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (NCRT) followed by esophagectomy remains standard for locally advanced resectable esophageal cancer. Active surveillance defers or avoids surgery in patients who meet clinical complete response (cCR) criteria. What that judgment rests on is fragile: cCR is assembled from whichever modality was used, at whatever time point, under whatever follow-up intensity. cCR is a clinical classification, whereas pathologic complete response (pCR) is established on a resection specimen. Endoscopy carries most of the weight, and observer-dependent interpretation remains a concern. We searched PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library from inception to 15 July 2026 and synthesized the findings narratively. Treatment settings differ enough to distort any pooled reading, so we stratified the evidence into four tiers-endoscopic AI in NCRT-treated cohorts, separated by pretreatment versus post-treatment image acquisition, conventional endoscopic and pathological response assessment, indirect AI evidence from neoadjuvant chemotherapy or immunotherapy, and other clinical and methodological context-rather than pooling it. Prediction model and diagnostic studies were independently appraised by two physicians using design-specific tools. Active surveillance achieved non-inferior two-year overall survival compared with immediate surgery in the SANO trial. preSINO measured how partial that reassurance is: bite-on-bite biopsy with endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration yielded a negative predictive value of 68.7% for residual disease. Among the seven endoscopy-based modeling reports summarized, one used pretreatment images in an NCRT cohort, and six were indirect studies from non-radiotherapy or predominantly non-radiotherapy cohorts. None separately validated AI on post-NCRT images for current residual disease detection. Most are retrospective, single-center, static image studies conducted in chemotherapy rather than chemoradiotherapy cohorts; the largest enrolled 1041 patients across 46 centers and reported 80% sensitivity and 90% specificity for primary site pCR, not patient-level ypT0N0. Patient-level sensitivity, negative predictive value, calibration, and decision curve analysis are seldom reported. Endoscopic AI belongs inside composite response assessment, as a second reader-not as the thing that decides whether surgery can be omitted or surveillance relaxed. The most informative study still unperformed is not another AUC comparison; it is a prospective trial adding AI-targeted sampling to systematic bite-on-bite biopsy, with the patient-level false-negative rate for residual disease as the primary endpoint. AI has the potential to standardize image interpretation; prospective reader studies are needed to establish reproducibility in practice. Whether it makes active surveillance safer is not yet known.

articles.title: Imaging- and Device-Based Congestion Assessment to Guide Chronic Heart Failure Management: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Congestion drives most heart-failure (HF) hospitalizations, and several strategies now titrate therapy to a directly measured congestion signal rather than to symptoms; whether they differ by the signal measured has not been examined comparatively. Methods: We performed a systematic review and contrast-based network meta-analysis of randomized trials comparing imaging- or device-based congestion-triggered management with usual care. Thirteen chronic-phase trials formed a star network (no closed loops; rankings exploratory) of four strategies, pressure-guided (N1), lung ultrasound (N2), transthoracic lung impedance (N3), and cardiac-implantable-electronic-device (CIED) intrathoracic impedance (N5), with HF hospitalization as the primary outcome and six prespecified sensitivity analyses; four acute trials formed a gap map. Results: Only pressure-guided monitoring reduced HF hospitalization (0.72, 95% confidence interval 0.57-0.90), stable across sensitivities and matching external data. Lung ultrasound did not reduce hospitalization (0.72, 0.48-1.08) or mortality but reduced urgent visits (0.26, 0.13-0.50). The apparent CIED-impedance harm (1.12, 0.77-1.63) reflected an audible-alert trial and dissolved when early-terminated trials were excluded (0.87). Lung impedance gave the largest estimate (0.51, 0.31-0.83) but rested on one trial. No strategy tested in more than one trial reduced mortality. Conclusions: The congestion signal acted upon, and who receives the alert, track with the effect, although signal and workflow cannot be separated within trials; clinicians should match modality to the intended outcome, as these tools defer hospitalization, not death.

articles.title: Circulating Non-Coding RNAs as Liquid Biopsy Biomarkers for Early Detection of Triple-Negative Breast Cancer: From Diagnostic Performance to Clinical Translation.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive and molecularly heterogeneous breast cancer subtype for which early detection remains clinically important. Circulating non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs), including microRNAs (miRNAs), long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), and circular RNAs (circRNAs), are being investigated as blood-based biomarkers. This narrative review evaluates the clinical evidence for circulating ncRNAs as liquid-biopsy biomarkers for early TNBC detection, focusing on stage I-II disease, diagnostic performance, comparator selection, and validation. Methods: Peer-reviewed studies published between 2009 and October 2026 were identified primarily through PubMed/MEDLINE searches, supplemented by Google Scholar searches, with particular attention to disease stage, comparator populations, diagnostic performance, and validation status. Results: Among the ncRNA classes reviewed, circulating miRNAs provide the most directly relevant, although still limited, clinical evidence for early-stage TNBC detection, whereas evidence for lncRNAs and circRNAs remains predominantly exploratory and insufficiently validated for early-stage detection. Translation is limited by small, heterogeneous cohorts, analytical variability, and insufficient independent and prospective validation. Conclusions: High diagnostic accuracy in selected cohorts does not establish clinical readiness. Standardized analytical workflows, independent multicenter validation, prospective evaluation in intended-use populations, and integration with imaging and clinical assessment are needed before circulating ncRNA signatures can be considered for clinical use.

articles.title: Lipidomics in Brain Health and Neurodegenerative Diseases: Mechanisms, Biomarkers, and Therapeutic Perspectives.
articles.abstract: Lipids constitute nearly half of the brain's dry weight and play a crucial role in maintaining the function of the central nervous system (CNS). Beyond their well-known function as structural components of cellular membranes and energy storage, lipids are now identified as dynamic bioactive mediators that regulate neuronal signaling, synaptic plasticity, membrane integrity and neuroinflammatory responses. Emerging evidence demonstrates that altered lipid homeostasis is associated with the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and Huntington's disease (HD). In this review, we highlight key pathophysiological mechanisms, including dysregulation of lipid transport by cholesterol and apolipoprotein E4 (ApoE4), which may influence the aggregation of amyloid-β in AD. We discuss sphingolipid dysregulation and impaired glucocerebrosidase activity in modulating α-synuclein pathology in PD. Furthermore, we emphasize the importance of polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) and their oxidized forms in the regulation of oxidative stress, ferroptosis, and neuronal cell death in ALS and HD. Besides mechanistic information, this review also highlights the recent advancements in modern lipidomic technologies, such as high-resolution mass spectrometry and multi-omics integration, which have facilitated the comprehensive characterization of disease-associated lipid alterations. Emerging lipid signatures, including alterations in ceramide, cholesterol metabolism and lipid droplet biogenesis in glial cells, are being investigated as candidate biomarkers and therapeutic targets. Collectively, we outline a strategy for exploiting the brain lipidome to explore the potential for personalized disease-modifying strategies against neurodegeneration by integrating mechanistic, diagnostic and therapeutic insights.

articles.title: Multidimensional Tracing of Error Sources and Structured Corrective Strategies for Leukocyte Count and Differential on Automated Hematology Analyzers.
articles.abstract: Leukocyte count and differential are core indicators for clinical infection assessment, hematological disease diagnosis, and therapeutic monitoring. Currently, clinical testing heavily relies on automated hematology analyzers. Influenced by factors such as specimen characteristics, limited analyzer recognition capability, and improper manual operations, automated testing often produces unreliable results, interfering with clinical decision-making and threatening patient safety. Existing studies remain fragmented, lacking a multidimensional error-tracing framework and practical corrective strategies covering the entire testing workflow. A narrative review was conducted to summarize the causes, identification methods, and corrective strategies for unreliable leukocyte results. Relevant literature up to August 2026 was searched in PubMed/MEDLINE and CNKI. We categorized multidimensional error sources into specimen-related interferents, leukocyte morphological and developmental abnormalities, and preanalytical or systematic factors, and established a practical diagnostic workflow spanning from anomaly recognition to result reporting. By incorporating both legacy and current analytical systems, we compared the characteristic scattergram patterns of various interferents across analyzers with different detection principles, broadening the applicability to diverse clinical laboratories. To better ensure the reliability of corrective strategies and provide diverse alternative options, we not only summarized widely accepted routine practices but also included case-based experimental methods. The proposed multidimensional error-tracing system and practical diagnostic workflow significantly improve analytical accuracy and reduce clinical risks. However, current hematology analyzers cannot automatically identify or correct complex interferences. Future systems must integrate multi-platform advantages, optimize complex cell recognition capabilities, and enrich multidimensional scattergram information to overcome existing analytical limitations. Furthermore, integrating artificial intelligence technology holds immense potential to drive automated hematology analysis toward a more intelligent and precise direction.

articles.title: Breathing at a Distance: Telemedicine's Achievements and Pitfalls in Respiratory Disease Management-A Narrative Review.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Telemedicine (TM) has become an increasingly important tool in the management of respiratory diseases, offering the potential to improve access to care, support long-term monitoring, and reduce the burden of in-person visits. This narrative review aims to critically summarize the current evidence on the achievements and limitations of TM across major areas of respiratory medicine. Methods: A non-systematic search of PubMed and Scopus was performed for English-language studies published up to April 2026, using combinations of keywords related to TM, telemonitoring, and respiratory diseases. Relevant articles were selected based on their clinical relevance and contribution to understanding the role of TM in diagnosis, monitoring, and management, and additional studies were identified through manual screening of reference lists. Results: The TM has shown consistent benefit for objective, device-derived outcomes-most notably CPAP adherence in obstructive sleep apnea-and for process outcomes such as reduced travel burden and improved cost-effectiveness primarily demonstrated in obstructive sleep apnea and COPD, with limited systematic evidence of cost-effectiveness in interstitial lung disease, home mechanical ventilation, cystic fibrosis, and smoking cessation. However, evidence for hard clinical endpoints such as hospitalization and mortality remains inconsistent, and successful implementation depends heavily on the surrounding care model rather than on technology alone. Conclusions: The TM represents a valuable complement to conventional respiratory care with demonstrated achievements in adherence, patient satisfaction, and healthcare efficiency, but its adoption remains limited by heterogeneous evidence, workforce and resource constraints, and the risk of widening digital disparities. Larger, adequately powered trials with harmonized outcomes and sustained investment in integrated care pathways are needed to fully realize its potential.

articles.title: Generative AI, Health Misinformation, and Medical Deepfakes: Implications for Diagnostic Safety and Clinical Practice-A Narrative Review.
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can rapidly produce persuasive health information in the form of text, synthetic images, cloned voices and deepfake videos. It can also be used to create fictitious professional identities. This narrative review describes how synthetic claims, fabricated evidence and simulated identities are used to disguise misleading health information and give it the appearance of authenticity especially with regard to diagnostic safety and clinical practice. Literature identified through Web of Science and Scopus was synthesized across text image audio video and multimodal formats; current evidence indicates that generative AI can produce highly credible but inaccurate health content. Source authority, message framing and professional identity cues influence trust and verification behavior, while disease-specific evaluations show that high average accuracy may coexist with clinically important omissions, missed referrals, hallucinated findings and poor calibration. In medical imaging, errors may arise both from incorrect interpretation and from manipulation of the diagnostic evidence itself. Detection, evidence-based verification, provenance, literacy interventions, and governance provide complementary safeguards, although real-world and longitudinal evidence remains limited. Clinical evaluation should therefore consider task-specific performance, source authenticity, human oversight, and the consequences of individual errors alongside overall accuracy.

articles.title: Prognostic Evidence for Artificial Intelligence-Derived PET Tumour-Burden Biomarkers in Cancer: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) can automate tumour-burden measurement on positron emission tomography (PET), including metabolic tumour volume (MTV) and total metabolic tumour volume (TMTV). This review evaluated prognostic evidence for AI-derived PET tumour-burden biomarkers, particularly comparisons with expert measurements. Methods: PubMed and Embase were searched on 29 August 2026; supplementary searching closed on 9 September. Revision follow-up used an export dated 13 October 2026 while retaining the original temporal eligibility boundary. English-language original reports evaluating AI-derived PET tumour burden and clinical outcomes were eligible. Core comparative and Contextual evidence were synthesized narratively by cancer, tracer, measurement, outcome and validation setting, accounting for shared cohorts. AI-assisted extraction and appraisal underwent human verification, without fully independent duplicate extraction or appraisal. Search coverage was incomplete, and no formal certainty-of-evidence grading was performed. The review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261497171). Results: We included 35 reports (13 Core and 22 Contextual) from 31 catalogue families; these families do not represent counts of independent validation cohorts. Selected studies reported associations between higher AI-derived MTV or TMTV and poorer outcomes, with confidence limited by confounding, threshold selection and validation design. Several reports found prognostic estimates similar to expert measurements without establishing equivalence. Heterogeneity in populations, outcomes, predictor scales and thresholds precluded pooled hazard ratios; incomplete paired uncertainty prevented pooling between-method differences. Of 62 prognostic factor assessment units, 37 had high risk of bias for confounding and 50 for statistical analysis and reporting. External validation of fixed prognostic thresholds remained limited. Conclusions: AI-derived MTV and TMTV showed prognostic associations in selected cancer settings, with limited confidence in their independence and transportability. Evidence does not establish interchangeability with expert measurements or improved outcomes from biomarker-guided treatment. Independent validation is needed before clinical use.

articles.title: Bronchiectasis in Systemic Autoimmune Rheumatic Diseases: Clinical Significance and Diagnostic Challenges.
articles.abstract: Bronchiectasis has been reported in several systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases, but published estimates are difficult to interpret because many studies count any bronchial dilatation on computed tomography (CT). This is particularly problematic in connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease (ILD), where traction can enlarge the airways without producing the clinical syndrome of bronchiectasis. We reviewed evidence in rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren disease, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody-associated vasculitis, systemic sclerosis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and inflammatory myopathies, with attention to imaging definitions, respiratory symptoms, infection, outcomes, and treatment. The association with a distinct airway disorder is best established in rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren disease, and myeloperoxidase-ANCA-positive vasculitis. In systemic sclerosis and systemic lupus erythematosus, large administrative cohorts suggest an increased occurrence of bronchiectasis, but most data do not allow for confident separation from traction bronchiectasis or other causes. In inflammatory myopathies, reported bronchial dilatation is mainly described within fibrotic ILD. In practice, interpretation should combine high-resolution CT morphology and distribution with cough and sputum, exacerbation history, microbiology, and the presence and extent of ILD; traction and non-traction changes may coexist. Bronchiectasis-specific care should follow established guidelines, while immunomodulatory therapy is selected for the rheumatic disease with explicit consideration of infection risk. No trial has identified a preferred antirheumatic regimen for patients with bronchiectasis, and it remains unknown whether better control of systemic disease changes bronchiectasis outcomes. Studies using consistent clinical and radiological definitions are needed. In mixed connective tissue disease, available evidence is insufficient to characterise bronchiectasis independently of ILD. Seven disease categories are reviewed in total.

articles.title: A Review of Machine Learning Approaches to Eye Disease Detection: Current Trends, Challenges and Future Directions.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Vision impairment and blindness remain a major global health challenge, with glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy, age-related macular degeneration, cataract, corneal disease, and retinopathy of prematurity representing important causes of preventable or treatable vision loss when detected early. This clinical need has accelerated research on machine learning approaches for automatic detection of eye diseases, grading, and segmentation. However, existing reviews often focus on a single disease or method. They also give limited attention to their suitability and applicability for reliable clinical deployments. This review synthesizes traditional machine learning, deep learning, vision transformers, ensemble and hybrid models, segmentation methods, and explainable AI approaches for eye disease detection. It further examines task formulation, dataset characteristics, evaluation practices, and deployment constraints, with emphasis on clinical readiness rather than benchmark performance alone. Methods: A structured narrative review was conducted using recently published articles from reputable databases and repositories, including IEEE Xplore, PubMed/MEDLINE, ScienceDirect, Scopus and arXiv. The review critically analyzes the progression from traditional machine learning to advanced models, including deep learning, vision transformers, ensemble models and explainable artificial intelligence. Studies were critically analyzed according to task formulations, dataset characteristics, segmentation approaches, evaluation metrics, explainability, and deployment constraints. Results: The synthesis shows that class imbalance, limited demographic and geographic diversity in available datasets, weak external validation, and scarce prospective evidence continue to separate benchmark performance from clinical readiness. Explainability is also often evaluated through visual plausibility rather than validated faithfulness. Currently, data-driven diabetic retinopathy screening is closest to clinical readiness, particularly for distinguishing referable from non-referable cases, whereas multi-label detection, rare disease detection, and cross-device deployment remain at the research stage. Conclusions: Progress towards clinical adoption requires stronger alignment between experimental evaluation and real-world deployment. This includes external validation and the development of equitable, interpretable, and resource-aware systems.

articles.title: Focused Cardiac Ultrasound and Doppler Hemodynamics in Nephrology Practice.
articles.abstract: Point-of-care ultrasonography (POCUS) in nephrology is evolving beyond kidney imaging and procedural guidance toward integrated hemodynamic assessment. Distinguishing reduced forward flow from elevated filling pressures and venous congestion remains challenging in patients with acute kidney injury and cardiorenal syndromes. This educational review discusses the clinical reasoning behind incorporating basic and advanced cardiac POCUS into nephrology practice. We highlight the interpretation and limitations of ventricular size and function, inferior vena cava assessment, stroke volume and left ventricular outflow tract Doppler, left ventricular filling pressures, right-sided and pulmonary artery pressures, and right ventricular outflow tract Doppler, with emphasis on how these findings may influence fluid removal, volume administration, and vasoactive therapy. The complementary role of venous excess ultrasound (VExUS) in assessing the downstream consequences of systemic venous congestion is also discussed. Rather than relying on isolated sonographic parameters or rigid cutoffs, cardiac POCUS findings should be integrated with multisystem ultrasound and the broader clinical context. Familiarity with these principles can help nephrologists obtain focused, repeatable hemodynamic information at the bedside and translate sonographic findings into more physiologically informed clinical decisions.

articles.title: Contrast-Enhanced Voiding Urosonography in Pediatric Vescicoureteral Reflux: A Narrative Review.
articles.abstract: Contrast-enhanced voiding urosonography (ceVUS) is a radiation-free technique for evaluating pediatric vesicoureteral reflux (VUR), although urethral catheterization is required. This narrative review summarizes its technical principles, diagnostic performance, safety, limitations, and clinical applications. Comparative studies suggest broadly similar diagnostic performance between ceVUS, voiding cystourethrography (VCUG), and direct radionuclide cystography; some report higher detection rates or reflux grading with ceVUS, but formal equivalence or superiority has not been established. Continuous real-time observation and repeated filling-voiding cycles may facilitate detection of intermittent reflux and intrarenal reflux, whereas grade I reflux confined to a non-dilated distal ureter may be missed. ceVUS-detected intrarenal reflux has shown a topographic association with acute cortical defects on dimercaptosuccinic acid scintigraphy, although its prognostic significance remains uncertain. Beyond initial diagnosis, ceVUS has been used for follow-up after conservative or surgical treatment, renal transplantation, and radiation-free videourodynamics. Intravesical second-generation microbubble agents have shown favorable short-term safety and parental acceptance. Nevertheless, evidence is limited by heterogeneous protocols, operator dependence, imperfect reference standards, and scarce data on clinical outcomes. Overall, ceVUS is a promising radiation-free option for selected pediatric VUR pathways, while fluoroscopic imaging remains appropriate when detailed urethral or complex distal ureteral anatomy is required.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence in Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia: From Prognostic Biomarkers to Individualized Treatment Selection.
articles.abstract: Available artificial intelligence (AI) applications in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) mainly address diagnosis, prognosis, treatment need, or measurable residual disease rather than comparative treatment selection. This state-of-the-art review examines the gap and proposes a CLL-specific clinical decision-support architecture. A focused evidence map was assembled by title-and-abstract screening of 245 unique PubMed records retrieved using a documented 2014-September 2026 search strategy. Fifty-five original CLL-relevant AI and machine learning (ML) reports were retained for descriptive mapping. Existing tools are heterogeneous and rarely establish comparative causal effects under competing regimens. We define individualized selection using clinically eligible treatment sets, explicit treatment contrasts, regimen-specific outcomes, calibration and uncertainty checks, and post hoc longitudinal patient-preference filtering. The architecture is conceptual, not a trained or externally validated treatment-selection algorithm; prospective studies will be necessary to demonstrate clinical utility.

articles.title: Postoperative Delirium Across the Perioperative Pathway: A Structured Narrative Review of Clinical Maturity and Implementation Priorities.
articles.abstract: Postoperative delirium (POD) is a highly prevalent but frequently underrecognized complication that disproportionately affects frail and older surgical patients. This structured narrative review aims to synthesize contemporary evidence on adult postoperative delirium across the perioperative pathway and to classify major preventive and therapeutic strategies according to clinical maturity, target population, and implementation readiness. A structured literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) and Web of Science Core Collection was performed, supplemented by ClinicalTrials.gov, official ESAIC and ASA resources, reference-list screening, and selected seminal pre-2021 publications. Current evidence supports a multifactorial model in which baseline cognitive and physiological vulnerability interacts with inflammatory, pharmacological, hemodynamic, nociceptive, sleep-related, and environmental stressors. No single anesthetic technique, processed-EEG target, blood-pressure threshold, cerebral oximetry strategy, or pharmacological agent consistently prevents POD across surgical populations. Multicomponent non-pharmacological prevention has the most consistent support, whereas dexmedetomidine and other pharmacological approaches appear context-dependent, and biomarkers and metabolic targets remain investigational. Future progress will depend on standardized delirium ascertainment, better phenotyping, multimodal prediction and prevention strategies, and reliable implementation systems that identify vulnerability early and maintain effective preventive care across transitions.

articles.title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Machine and Deep Learning Methods in Intracranial Hemorrhage Detection: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: In this systematic review we investigated the diagnostic accuracy of machine and deep learning algorithms for the detection of intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) and its subtypes such as subarachnoid, intraventricular, intraparenchymal, subdural and epidural hemorrhage. In addition, we investigated their generalizability by comparing methods tested on private vs. public datasets, and FDA- vs. non-FDA-approved algorithms. Methods: PubMed, Scopus and Embase were searched between January 2010 and December 2025. Eligible studies included patients with acute neurological deficit that received non-contrast CT head scans and implemented machine and deep learning algorithms for ICH detection, that were tested on private and/or public datasets, received FDA approval or not, and used clinicians' evaluation as reference standard. Pooled sensitivity and specificity were incorporated for meta-analysis. Results: A total of 89 publications received full assessment and 51 studies were included in the meta-analysis. The pooled sensitivity and specificity for ICH detection were 94.5% (95% CI: 92.4-96.0) and 95.3% (95% CI: 93.1-96.9), respectively. For AI methods tested on private and public datasets, the pooled sensitivity reached 94.4% (95% CI: 91.2-96.5) and 94.5% (95% CI: 91.8-96.4), with a pooled specificity in 95.6% (95% CI: 92.9-97.2) and 95.1% (95% CI: 90.1-97.5), respectively. FDA- and non-FDA-approved AI algorithms showed a pooled sensitivity of 90.7% (95% CI: 87.1-93.4) and specificity of 95.8% (95% CI: 90.3-98.3) in the former group, and 95.5% (95% CI: 93.4-96.9) and 95.7% (95% CI: 92.4-97.6) for the latter group. Conclusions: Study results demonstrated that the diagnostic accuracy of the developed AI algorithms for ICH detection is equivalent to that of experienced clinicians. Methods tested on private and public datasets, and FDA- vs. non-FDA-approved, differ slightly in ICH diagnosis, showing encouraging signs for their incorporation in decision support systems in stroke patient pathways.

articles.title: Scoring Systems in Pyogenic Spondylodiscitis-A Narrative Review.
articles.abstract: Background: Pyogenic spondylodiscitis has become increasingly common over the past two decades, and its nonspecific presentation, together with frequent diagnostic delay, makes severity assessment, prognosis, and surgical decision-making difficult to standardize based on clinical judgement alone. Methods: This narrative review was based on a targeted literature search through August 2026, combining terms for spondylodiscitis and vertebral osteomyelitis with the names of individually identified scoring systems and validation-related terms, distinguishing development from reliability testing and independent external validation. Results: Several disease-specific tools addressing severity, prognosis, or the decision to operate were identified. The most extensively evaluated treatment-decision tool showed moderate-to-good, if variable, performance across cohorts, while another frequently cited score performed less consistently in an independent population. One severity classification showed confirmed reliability but more limited predictive evidence, and mortality-prediction tools remain independently unvalidated. Conclusions: No single system currently demonstrates consistent performance across severity assessment, prognosis, and surgical decision-making. Existing tools should therefore be applied within the specific clinical context for which they were developed, while further independent external validation is needed before broader clinical implementation.

articles.title: Microinvasive Cervical Cancer as a Model for Therapeutic De-Escalation in Gynecologic Oncology.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Microinvasive cervical cancer represents the earliest stage of stromal invasion and is associated with excellent oncological outcomes. Its clinical relevance arises from the potential disproportion between the limited extent of invasive disease and the morbidity of radical treatment, particularly in young women wishing to preserve fertility. Increasing evidence supports a transition from stage-based surgical radicality toward individualized, risk-adapted management. This narrative review critically examines microinvasive cervical cancer as a distinct clinical model of therapeutic de-escalation, with particular attention to the boundaries between evidence-supported conservative treatment and areas in which uncertainty persists. METHODS: A narrative review of PubMed/MEDLINE was conducted for studies published between January 2010 and March 2026. Evidence concerning FIGO stages IA1 and IA2 was analyzed, focusing on diagnostic conization, pathological risk factors, lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI), margin status, histological subtype, fertility-sparing treatment, sentinel lymph node (SLN) assessment, ultrastaging, and follow-up. Studies including broader early-stage cervical cancer populations were considered only when stage IA results were separately available or clinically transferable to microinvasive disease, and were interpreted as indirect evidence when appropriate. RESULTS: Accurate conization represents the cornerstone of the diagnosis and initial risk stratification of microinvasive cervical cancer, providing essential information on depth of stromal invasion, margin status, LVSI, histological subtype and multifocality. However, optimal risk assessment should integrate pathological findings with clinical staging, appropriate imaging and, when indicated, nodal assessment. FIGO stage alone does not adequately define individual risk, while imaging itself cannot reliably exclude occult small-volume nodal disease; therefore, the relative contribution of pathology, imaging and surgical nodal staging should be tailored to the individual risk profile. In FIGO IA1 disease without LVSI and with negative margins, conization alone provides excellent oncological control and lymph node staging is generally unnecessary. LVSI should be considered a risk modifier that may influence nodal assessment rather than an automatic indication for more radical cervical surgery. In IA1 with LVSI and IA2 disease, SLN biopsy may provide nodal staging with lower morbidity than systematic lymphadenectomy, although evidence specifically generated in microinvasive tumors remains limited. Fertility-sparing treatment is oncologically appropriate in carefully selected patients, whereas simple hysterectomy represents an adequate definitive option after completion of reproductive plans. Microinvasive adenocarcinoma requires specific consideration because of its endocervical location, potential multifocality, and the biological distinction between HPV-associated and HPV-independent histotypes. Major uncertainties remain regarding the prognostic significance of LVSI and low-volume nodal disease, the optimal indications for SLN assessment, and the limits of exclusive conservative treatment in IA2 disease. CONCLUSIONS: Microinvasive cervical cancer should not be regarded simply as the earliest anatomical stage of cervical cancer, but as a distinct clinical setting in which diagnostic precision may enable oncologically safe therapeutic de-escalation. The available evidence supports a shift from maximum surgical radicality toward the minimum effective treatment, provided that accurate histopathological assessment, appropriate patient selection, and specialized follow-up are ensured. Importantly, several recommendations for stage IA-particularly for IA2 disease and nodal management-still rely partly on evidence extrapolated from broader early-stage cervical cancer populations. Prospective multicenter studies and dedicated stage IA registries are therefore needed to define more precisely the boundaries within which therapeutic de-escalation can be safely applied.

articles.title: Multimodal In Vivo Imaging of Cutaneous Angiogenesis: A Structured Narrative Review of Dermoscopy, Dynamic OCT, and Line-Field Confocal OCT.
articles.abstract: Aims: This structured narrative review aimed to synthesize and critically appraise the available human evidence on in vivo assessment of cutaneous angiogenesis using dermoscopy, dynamic optical coherence tomography (D-OCT), and line-field confocal optical coherence tomography (LC-OCT), and to determine whether disease-specific microvascular phenotypes can be defined across selected neoplastic and inflammatory dermatoses. Type of review. Structured narrative review (SNAR), using SANRA as a narrative-review quality framework. The work was not designed as a systematic review of diagnostic accuracy and was not prospectively registered. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from inception to November 2025 using combinations of terms for angiogenesis, cutaneous vasculature, dermoscopy, OCT, D-OCT, LC-OCT, OCT angiography, melanoma, basal cell carcinoma, actinic keratosis, squamous neoplasia, Bowen disease, psoriasis, and Kaposi sarcoma. The clinical synthesis focused on original human studies; technical reviews and preclinical sources were used for background only. Findings: Findings were synthesized qualitatively because imaging protocols and vascular terminology were too heterogeneous for meta-analysis. Salient findings. Angiogenic architecture is disease-patterned rather than uniform. D-OCT studies associate melanoma vascular morphology with Breslow thickness, without establishing a validated optical staging test. Basal cell carcinoma shows hierarchically organized arborizing stromal vessels. Bowen disease shows glomerular, horizontally oriented units, whereas actinic keratosis shows milder, grade-dependent remodeling; multimodal imaging remains limited in separating hypertrophic actinic keratosis from early squamous cell carcinoma. Psoriasis shows elongated, regularly distributed dilated papillary loops, distinct from the less organized pattern of eczematous dermatitis. Kaposi sarcoma imaging evidence remains preliminary and does not establish stage-specific vascular criteria. Plexus depth is measurable and differs among some diseases and adjacent skin, but it is not a standalone marker of invasiveness. LC-OCT adds near-histologic three-dimensional morphology; D-OCT adds perfusion and depth; dermoscopy remains the accessible surface map. Conclusions: Multimodal in vivo imaging can link surface vascular clues to structural and functional substrates of cutaneous angiogenesis and can improve interpretive separation of disease-specific patterns from non-specific inflammatory remodeling. Most proposed quantitative biomarkers, including plexus depth, remain preliminary and require standardized descriptors and prospective multicenter validation, including studies with inflamed mimics, before routine clinical use.

articles.title: Per-Patient Polyp Detection Rate of Colon Capsule Endoscopy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis with Exploratory Stratification by Referral Pathway.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Colon capsule endoscopy (CCE) is a minimally invasive alternative to optical colonoscopy, but per-patient polyp detection rate (PDR), the proportion of patients with at least one visually reported polyp, varies across referral populations. We estimated any-polyp and size-stratified CCE yield and explored between-study variation. Methods: MEDLINE, Embase, PubMed, and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched from 1 January 2004 to 29 July 2026. Proportions were pooled using random-intercept binomial-normal generalised linear mixed models. PROSPERO: CRD420261464937 (registration not prospective). Results: Of 44 retained studies (12,754 participants), 31 independent studies (11,310 participants) formed the primary pool. Pooled PDR was 53.2% (95% CI 46.1-60.1; prediction interval 19-85%), a descriptive average, not a performance target. Exploratory PDR was 81.2% after positive FIT (k = 4), 49.4% after incomplete colonoscopy (k = 4), and 39.9% in screening without prior FIT enrichment (k = 3); 14 studies had mixed pathways. Pooled detection was 32.7% for polyps ≥ 6 mm (prediction interval 8-74%) and 17.7% for polyps ≥ 10 mm (4-51%). Conclusions: CCE PDR is a visual yield measure, not adenoma detection or diagnostic accuracy. A global CCE PDR is not a portable quality threshold; referral-pathway estimates are descriptive and hypothesis-generating. Future quality metrics require standardised pathways, denominators, and linkage to downstream clinical outcomes.

articles.title: Compartmentalization of Host Multi-Omics Responses in Lower Respiratory Tract Infection: Discordance Between Airway-Local and Systemic Molecular Profiles-A Narrative Review.
articles.abstract: Lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) remains a leading cause of infection-related mortality. Peripheral blood multi-omics shows promise for pathogen discrimination and severity prediction, yet how well blood reflects airway-local responses in LRTI other than coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) is unclear. We searched PubMed, Web of Science Core Collection, and Europe PMC (January 2021 to August 2026); after de-duplication and dual screening, 29 of 817 unique records were included (Layer A: ≥2 host functional omics layers, n = 23; Layer B: single omics platform with paired airway-blood specimens, n = 6), plus four COVID-19 benchmarks. Blood-based multi-omics distinguished bacterial, viral, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae (M. pneumoniae) LRTI; severity models performed promisingly within their discovery cohorts. In the two studies reporting airway-versus-blood protein inventories, the airway showed more differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) than blood (airway-to-blood DEP count ratios ≈ 3.6-9.3; descriptive study-specific measures), and cross-compartment correlations were predominantly weak (r ≈ -0.3 to +0.3) in the only paired viral LRTI study; interferon-stimulated gene 15 (ISG15; r = 0.79) was a notable exception. Paired evidence derives mostly from a pediatric cohort, hospital-acquired pneumonia, and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS); adult community-acquired LRTI remains under-represented. Current evidence suggests that peripheral blood provides an incomplete, context-dependent representation of airway-local responses; closing this gap requires adult longitudinal paired cohorts, non-invasive airway sampling, improved integration algorithms, and multimodal data fusion.

articles.title: Persistent High-Risk HPV Positivity Without Confirmed CIN2+: Diagnostic Uncertainty, Risk Stratification, and Management-A Narrative Review.
articles.abstract: Primary high-risk human papillomavirus (hrHPV) testing detects cervical precancer earlier than cytology and, by design, generates a large population of virus-positive women in whom high-grade disease is not confirmed. Where the infection persists, the clinician must judge whether a negative or non-diagnostic assessment reflects absence of disease or failure of detection. This review asks what that state represents, which tools reclassify absolute CIN3+ risk, and how surveillance and intervention should be balanced. This narrative review synthesises relevant evidence from published studies and international guidance on persistent hrHPV infection, diagnostic assessment, risk stratification and management, with reporting guided by the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA). Persistent hrHPV positivity without confirmed CIN2+ is a heterogeneous risk state, not a diagnosis, and covers three clinical situations that should not be conflated. Absolute CIN3+ risk is set principally by genotype and by the duration of type-specific persistence; genotype alone spans an approximately twenty-fold range of immediate risk in hrHPV-positive screening populations. Pooled colposcopic sensitivity for CIN2+ was approximately 75% in heterogeneous referral populations, while one selected retrospective series of cytology-negative hrHPV-positive women reported sensitivity near 50%. Selected referral cohorts have reported CIN2+/HSIL detection yields of approximately 8% to 14% among persistently hrHPV-positive women with normal cytology; these composite, selection-dependent estimates should not be read as the prevalence of occult CIN3+. Extended genotyping and p16/Ki-67 dual-stain cytology carry guideline-adopted management rules, although validation specifically after documented persistence remains limited. Controlled evidence for treating persistent hrHPV without confirmed CIN2+ is sparse and conflicting. Recent randomised trials of vaginal interventions report discordant short-term virological results, and none establishes durable clearance or a reduction in CIN3+ risk. Short-term loss of HPV detectability is not equivalent to prevention of precancer, and management should remain risk-based.

articles.title: Beyond LDL-C: Biomarker-Informed Risk Assessment and Management of Residual Cardiovascular Risk in the Era of Precision Prevention.
articles.abstract: Despite substantial reductions in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) events with intensive low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) lowering, considerable residual cardiovascular risk persists among individuals achieving guideline-recommended LDL-C targets. This residual risk reflects biological pathways not addressed by LDL-C lowering and remains a central challenge in preventive cardiology. This narrative review examines three overlapping domains: residual lipid risk related to triglyceride-rich lipoprotein remnants and excess apolipoprotein B-containing particles; genetically determined lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)]-mediated risk; and residual inflammatory risk involving the NLRP3 inflammasome and downstream interleukin-1β and interleukin-6 signaling. Complementary biomarkers, including apolipoprotein B, non-HDL cholesterol, remnant cholesterol, Lp(a), and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, may help characterize residual-risk phenotypes beyond LDL-C alone, although their incremental value and influence on management vary with the strength of prognostic and causal evidence and the availability of effective therapies. Icosapent ethyl and low-dose colchicine have demonstrated cardiovascular benefit in selected high-risk populations, whereas the cardiovascular benefits of therapies targeting apoC-III, ANGPTL3, and Lp(a) remain under evaluation. Recent phase 3 findings have further underscored uncertainty regarding the cardiovascular benefit of interleukin-6 inhibition. Integrating complementary biomarkers with therapies supported by randomized outcomes evidence may enable a more individualized approach to residual cardiovascular risk reduction.

articles.title: Functional Recovery After Alcohol Septal Ablation for Hypertrophic Obstructive Cardiomyopathy-When Measured Success Does Not Equal Complete Recovery.
articles.abstract: Alcohol septal ablation (ASA) is an established septal reduction therapy for symptomatic patients with hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM). Although successful treatment is traditionally defined by a reduction in left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction and improvement in symptoms, these parameters do not necessarily indicate complete functional recovery. Persistent exercise intolerance may occur despite an apparently successful intervention, reflecting the complex pathophysiology of HCM. This review explores the mechanisms underlying incomplete functional recovery after ASA and evaluates contemporary approaches to objectively assess treatment response. Functional capacity after ASA is determined by multiple interacting factors, including residual or recurrent LVOT obstruction, abnormal mitral and papillary muscle anatomy, persistent diastolic dysfunction, myocardial fibrosis, valvular disease, pulmonary hypertension, and coronary microvascular dysfunction. Age, deconditioning, pulmonary disease, anemia, musculoskeletal limitations, and other comorbidities may independently contribute to exercise intolerance. Conventional assessment based on New York Heart Association functional class and resting echocardiography may therefore underestimate persistent physiological impairment. Cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) provides a comprehensive assessment of exercise capacity by integrating cardiovascular, pulmonary, and metabolic responses. Exercise echocardiography, cardiac magnetic resonance, pulmonary function testing, and, in selected patients, invasive exercise hemodynamics provide complementary information. Emerging strategies including multimodality imaging, pharmacological therapy, individualized rehabilitation, and wearable activity monitoring may further improve assessment and long-term recovery. Conclusions: Successful reduction in LVOT obstruction after ASA should not be considered synonymous with complete functional recovery. A multimodality, physiology-oriented approach, with CPET as a central objective tool, may better identify residual limitations and guide individualized management. Future studies should focus on physiological rather than purely anatomical endpoints and determine whether patient selection, procedural precision, and phenotype-guided rehabilitation can improve functional recovery after ASA.

articles.title: Can Ocular Optical Biomarkers Predict Response to Contact-Lens Myopia Control? A Critical Review of Current Evidence.
articles.abstract: Background: Contact-lens interventions can slow, but do not arrest, axial elongation in children, and individual response varies substantially. The review examined whether early optical measurements of the lens-eye system can provide clinically useful prediction of later axial growth. Methods: A critical narrative review of PubMed-indexed literature was updated through October 2026. Evidence from dual-focus, centre-distance multifocal and extended-depth-of-focus soft contact lenses and orthokeratology was appraised according to temporal ordering, repeatability, independent prediction, external validation and potential clinical utility. Spectacle-based myopia-control designs were outside the primary scope. Results: Relative peripheral refraction (RPR), pupil-weighted retinal image-quality metrics and selected higher-order aberration (HOA) measures are the principal optical candidates. In soft-lens wear, early wide-field RPR change has shown moderate discrimination of later axial growth. In orthokeratology, the most developed HOA evidence concerns total HOA root-mean-square (RMS), primary spherical aberration and coma; change in total anterior corneal HOA RMS has shown the strongest single-study discrimination. Accommodation, lens centration, pupil size and wear time are better treated as modifiers of optical exposure than as ocular optical biomarkers. Positive findings remain largely small, single-centre, post hoc or design-specific, and no candidate has undergone adequate independent external validation. Conclusions: Current evidence supports candidate-predictive signals rather than clinically validated biomarkers. No optical measure has demonstrated sufficient incremental value beyond established clinical factors or shown that biomarker-guided management improves outcomes. Modality-specific or multivariable optical signatures remain more plausible than a universal scalar marker.

articles.title: Prognostic Value of the KELIM Score Versus Conventional CA-125 Kinetics in Ovarian Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: To compare the prognostic value of the modeled cancer antigen-125 (CA-125) elimination rate constant K (KELIM) with that of conventional CA-125 kinetics (e.g., half-life) in epithelial ovarian cancer. Methods: PubMed, EMBASE, and Cochrane CENTRAL were searched from inception to 8 July 2026, using terms for ovarian cancer, CA-125 kinetics (KELIM, half-life, nadir), platinum-based chemotherapy, and survival or cytoreduction. Hazard ratios (HRs) and odds ratios (ORs) were pooled using random-effects models. Results: Thirty-seven studies were included (KELIM, 29; conventional, 8). Favorable KELIM was associated with longer overall survival (HR: 0.54, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.47-0.63; 14 cohorts; I2 = 72%; moderate certainty) and progression-free survival (HR: 0.57, 95% CI: 0.51-0.63; 18 cohorts; I2 = 62%) and with complete cytoreduction (OR: 3.34, 95% CI: 2.00-5.55; nine cohorts). Short CA-125 half-life was associated with longer overall survival (HR: 0.48, 95% CI: 0.38-0.60; three cohorts; low certainty); no study assessed both markers in the same cohort. Sensitivity analyses changed the estimates little. Conclusions: KELIM is a consistent prognostic factor in ovarian cancer. Its similarity to CA-125 half-life rests on an indirect comparison with older cohorts and does not establish equivalence or superiority. Evidence that KELIM predicts treatment benefit remains exploratory.

articles.title: Germline AIP Testing in Pituitary Neuroendocrine Tumors: Diagnostic Yield, Variant Interpretation, and a Phenotype-Driven Clinical Approach-A Narrative Review.
